title: Functions, fibers and equivalence
description: Explain a fiber; distinguish an inverse image from an inverse; test independence of representatives.
entryCompetencies: Read set membership and compose two functions.
outcomes: distinguish an inverse image from an inverse

capstone.question: For f: Z → Z/3Z, describe every fiber. Does [n] modulo 3 ↦ [n²] modulo 6 define a function? Compare n=0 and n=3.
capstone.answer: Fibers are residue classes modulo 3. The proposed rule fails because 0 and 3 represent the same input but their squares are 0 and 3 modulo 6.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Operations and groups
description: Verify group axioms and distinguish order from cardinality.
entryCompetencies: Recognise a function and compose maps.
outcomes: Verify group axioms and distinguish order from cardinality.

capstone.question: Compare addition on Z with subtraction on Z. Derive (ab)⁻¹ and test the formula on triangle motions.
capstone.answer: Subtraction fails associativity and has no two-sided identity. Since (ab)(b⁻¹a⁻¹)=e=(b⁻¹a⁻¹)(ab), the inverse is b⁻¹a⁻¹.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Subgroups, generators and cyclic structure
description: Find generated subgroups and orders of powers.
outcomes: Find generated subgroups and orders of powers.

capstone.question: List all subgroups of C12 and determine which contain g⁴. Explain the reversed divisibility relation.
capstone.answer: The subgroups are generated by gᵈ for d=1,2,3,4,6,12. Those containing g⁴ have d dividing 4: 1,2,4. The order of gᵈ is 12/d.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Cosets and Lagrange
description: Partition a group into equal cosets and test normality.
outcomes: Partition a group into equal cosets and test normality.

capstone.question: Partition S3 by H={e,(12)}. Can its three cosets form a quotient group with representative multiplication?
capstone.answer: The left cosets partition six elements into three pairs. H is not normal: (123)(12)(123)⁻¹=(23) is outside H. Hence the proposed quotient operation is not well-defined.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Homomorphisms, kernels and quotients
description: Prove quotient maps are well-defined and identify kernels and images.
outcomes: Prove quotient maps are well-defined and identify kernels and images.

capstone.question: Use the sign map S3 → {±1} to construct S3/A3 and prove its identification with C2.
capstone.answer: Sign is a surjective homomorphism with kernel A3. Equal cosets have equal signs; equal signs differ by an element of A3. Thus gA3 ↦ sign(g) is a well-defined bijective homomorphism.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Actions and orbit–stabilizer
description: Compute orbit, stabilizer and kernel without confusing them.
outcomes: Compute orbit, stabilizer and kernel without confusing them.

capstone.question: For S3 acting on three letters, compute the orbit and stabilizer of 1 and the action kernel. Is a point stabilizer the kernel?
capstone.answer: The orbit is {1,2,3}; the stabilizer is {e,(23)}; the kernel is {e}. Orbit size times stabilizer size is 3·2=6. A stabilizer fixes one point, the kernel fixes every point.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Counting with group actions
description: Count orbits with a fixed-point table and explain the averaging argument.
entryCompetencies: Compute fixed points of a permutation.
outcomes: Count orbits with a fixed-point table and explain the averaging argument.

capstone.question: Count binary necklaces of length 4 under rotations, including the constant necklaces.
capstone.answer: The four rotations fix 16,2,4,2 colorings. Their average is 6. Reflections are excluded; including them changes the acting group and requires another fixed-point table.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Cauchy and Sylow theory
description: Separate existence, conjugacy and arithmetic constraints.
outcomes: Separate existence, conjugacy and arithmetic constraints.

capstone.question: Prove every group of order 15 is cyclic, identifying each use of a Sylow theorem.
capstone.answer: n5 divides 3 and is 1 modulo 5, so n5=1. n3 divides 5 and is 1 modulo 3, so n3=1. The normal Sylow subgroups intersect trivially and commute; their product is C3 × C5 ≅ C15.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Rings, ideals and quotient rings
description: Distinguish subrings from ideals and units from nonzero elements.
entryCompetencies: Use additive groups and well-defined quotient rules.
outcomes: Distinguish subrings from ideals and units from nonzero elements.

capstone.question: Determine the units and zero divisors of Z/12Z. Identify the kernel and image of reduction to Z/4Z.
capstone.answer: Units are 1,5,7,11. Nonzero zero divisors are 2,3,4,6,8,9,10. Reduction has kernel {0,4,8} and image Z/4Z; the first isomorphism theorem identifies the quotient by that kernel.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Factorisation and polynomial rings
description: Distinguish roots, reducibility and coefficient-field hypotheses.
entryCompetencies: Understand domains, units and polynomial degree.
outcomes: Distinguish roots, reducibility and coefficient-field hypotheses.

capstone.question: Compare x²+1 over Q, R, C and F2. Explain why a root test alone fails for degree 4.
capstone.answer: It is irreducible over Q and R, splits as (x−i)(x+i) over C, and equals (x+1)² over F2. A degree-4 polynomial can split into two quadratics without linear roots.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Localisation and chain conditions
description: Identify inverted elements and distinguish chain stabilization from finite cardinality.
outcomes: Identify inverted elements and distinguish chain stabilization from finite cardinality.

capstone.question: In Z localized at (3), decide whether 2 and 3 are units. Is Z Noetherian despite being infinite?
capstone.answer: 2 is a unit since its denominator is allowed; 3 is not. Every ideal of Z is principal, hence Z is Noetherian; Noetherian concerns chains of ideals, not cardinality.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Modules, generators and exactness
description: Describe a scalar action, nonfree presentation and exact sequence.
entryCompetencies: Use abelian groups, ring maps and linear maps.
outcomes: Describe a scalar action, nonfree presentation and exact sequence.

capstone.question: Give a presentation and annihilator of Z/6Z as a Z-module and explain why multiplication by 2 on Z/3Z is invertible.
capstone.answer: Z/6Z has one generator with relation 6e=0 and annihilator 6Z; 0 → Z → Z → Z/6Z → 0 is exact when the first map multiplies by 6. On Z/3Z, multiplication by 2 is its own inverse, despite 2 not being a unit of Z.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Representations and invariant subspaces
description: Test invariant subspaces and intertwining maps.
entryCompetencies: Use bases, kernels and matrix multiplication on columns.
outcomes: Test invariant subspaces and intertwining maps.

capstone.question: Split the complex permutation representation of S3 on C³ into its constant line and sum-zero plane. Verify both subspaces are invariant.
capstone.answer: Coordinate permutations preserve constant vectors and coordinate sums. Their intersection is zero over C and dimensions add to 3, giving a direct sum of invariant subspaces. The projection onto constants averages the three coordinates.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Maschke, Schur and characters
description: Use averaging and distinguish real from complex irreducibility.
outcomes: Use averaging and distinguish real from complex irreducibility.

capstone.question: Compute the character of the sum-zero S3 representation on identity, transposition and 3-cycle. Explain its degree and field.
capstone.answer: Over C the sum-zero plane has dimension 2. Subtract the constant character from the three-point permutation character: (3,1,0)−(1,1,1)=(2,0,−1). Maschke applies since characteristic zero does not divide 6.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Character tables and decomposition
description: Construct S3 irreducibles and decompose a character using class sizes.
entryCompetencies: Compute traces and weighted inner products.
outcomes: Construct S3 irreducibles and decompose a character using class sizes.

capstone.question: Decompose the S3 character (5,1,−1) against trivial, sign and standard characters using class sizes 1,3,2.
capstone.answer: The inner products are 1,0,2, respectively. Thus the representation is one trivial copy plus two standard copies, of dimension 1+2·2=5.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Tensor and direct-product representations
description: Distinguish tensor balancing from external tensor products and test faithfulness.
entryCompetencies: Understand multilinearity and the complex S3 standard representation.
outcomes: Distinguish tensor balancing from external tensor products and test faithfulness.

capstone.question: Explain why two faithful factors can yield a nonfaithful external tensor product using scalar −I.
capstone.answer: On C2 take its faithful sign character; on D8 take its faithful complex two-dimensional square representation. The nonidentity pair (−1,r²) acts as (−1)⊗(−I)=I, so the product has nontrivial kernel.
